# Results — Study 938 (Open or Close) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One rule, two fills. The rule is
the plain moving-average timing filter — hold the ETF while its period-end close is above the
mean of the last `L` period-end closes, else hold **BIL** (1-3 month T-bills) — run in two
flavours: **10-month** (rebalanced at month ends) and **20-week** (rebalanced at week ends).
Long-only and binary, so there is **no short leg and no borrow cost**. The signal is formed
from data through the close of the rebalance day `t`; **both arms fill on `t+1`** (exactly one
execution lag). They differ only in where: the `open` arm fills at the **open of `t+1`**, the
`close` arm at the **close of `t+1`**. Costs are **2 bps one-way × NAV** on both venues.
Daily **adjusted** OHLC (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`): the intraday leg (open → close) is
**price-only**, the overnight leg carries the dividend, and their product is the close-to-close
**total** return. Window gated by BIL's 2007-05-30 inception. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial
current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY, IWM, EEM, EFA (risk) + BIL (cash) | 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30 | 4,802 | Fingerprint `f36d90ae4fdc` |

**Non-tape inputs (labelled PROXY / ASSUMPTION, both swept below):** (1) the *extra* one-way
cost of filling in the opening auction rather than the closing auction — set to **0 bps** in
the headline and swept to +5 bps; (2) the share of the cash leg's daily accrual booked to the
overnight leg — **0.73** (17.5h of 24h), swept 0 → 1.

## The gap is confined to trade days

On every non-trade day the two arms hold the identical book, so the whole difference is one
thin sliver: on each trade day the arms differ by `Δweight × (asset intraday − cash intraday)`.
The rules trade rarely (31–37 times in 19 years monthly, 88–114 weekly), so the question is not
"is the intraday drift positive" — it is "is the intraday move on *entry* days systematically
different from the one on *exit* days".

## Rule A — the 10-month filter (month-end rebalance)

| Tape | trades | Gap (open − close) | HAC *t* | Per-trade | Open wins | exSharpe open / close |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 31 | −4.8 bps/yr | −0.16 | −2.9 bps | 45% | +0.587 / +0.589 |
| IWM | 37 | +50.7 bps/yr | +1.04 | +25.1 bps | 59% | +0.363 / +0.331 |
| EEM | 37 | **+66.6 bps/yr** | **+2.40** | +32.9 bps | 70% | +0.313 / +0.270 |
| EFA | 33 | +35.4 bps/yr | +1.69 | +19.6 bps | 61% | +0.299 / +0.272 |
| **Pooled (equal-weight)** | — | **+37.0 bps/yr** | **+1.53** | — | — | +0.444 / +0.413 |

Pooled gross = pooled net (both venues pay the same 2 bps). Block-bootstrap 95% CI on the
pooled gap **[−12.0, +85.3] bps/yr** (6.8% of draws negative). **Excess-of-cash** CAGR +4.90%
(open) vs +4.51% (close) — raw, cash-inclusive +6.21% vs +5.82%; the Sharpes above are built
on the excess series, and the two growth rates are labelled apart everywhere. Only **one** of
the four tapes clears |*t*| = 2 — EEM, on 37 trades.

## Rule B — the 20-week filter (week-end rebalance, ~3× the trades)

| Tape | trades | Gap (open − close) | HAC *t* | Per-trade | Open wins | exSharpe open / close |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 88 | −35.8 bps/yr | −0.81 | −7.6 bps | 50% | +0.588 / +0.615 |
| IWM | 114 | −19.0 bps/yr | −0.29 | −3.1 bps | 46% | +0.382 / +0.392 |
| EEM | 102 | −26.2 bps/yr | −0.54 | −4.8 bps | 45% | +0.333 / +0.349 |
| EFA | 96 | −23.4 bps/yr | −0.66 | −4.6 bps | 45% | +0.412 / +0.432 |
| **Pooled (equal-weight)** | — | **−26.1 bps/yr** | **−0.80** | — | — | +0.494 / +0.515 |

Bootstrap CI **[−90.9, +35.7] bps/yr** (80.7% of draws negative). **Excess-of-cash** CAGR
+5.27% (open) vs +5.54% (close) — raw, cash-inclusive +6.64% vs +6.92%. The higher-powered
rule prints the **opposite sign** to the monthly one, on the same four tapes over the same
window. *Caveat on the comparison:* 20 weeks (~100 sessions) is a **shorter** lookback than 10
months (~210), so Rule B is faster **and** shorter-horizon — not a pure change of execution
frequency. It buys the power; it is not a clean replication of Rule A.

## The whole tape in one line

Pool every fill from both rules and all four tapes — **538 trades**:

| | value |
|---|--:|
| Mean slippage per trade (open − close) | **+1.39 bps** |
| *t*, naive (treats every fill as independent) | +0.33 |
| ***t*, clustered on the trade date** | **+0.23** |
| Open-fill wins | 267 / 538 = **49.6%** |
| 95% Wilson interval on the win rate (assumes independence) | [45.4%, 53.8%] |
| **95% cluster-bootstrap interval** (resamples whole trade dates) | **[44.1%, 55.1%]** |
| 95% cluster-bootstrap interval on the mean slippage | **[−10.8, +13.0] bps** |

**The 538 fills are not 538 independent draws** and this study does not pretend otherwise:
SPY / IWM / EEM / EFA are highly correlated and their moving-average signals flip on the same
days, so the fills sit on only **361 distinct dates**, and the two rules share one window. The
naive *t* and the Wilson interval both assume that away; clustering on the trade date drops the
*t* to **+0.23** and widens the win-rate interval to **[44.1%, 55.1%]**. Every correction
pushes the same way — further into "coin flip" — which is why the stamp does not move.

## Robustness

**Two eras (split 2017-01-01), pooled book:**

| Rule | 2007–2016 | 2017–2026 |
|---|--:|--:|
| 10-month | +57.4 bps/yr (*t* = +1.96) | +17.9 bps/yr (*t* = +0.47) |
| 20-week | +27.2 bps/yr (*t* = +0.58) | **−78.0 bps/yr** (*t* = −1.73) |

The two rules disagree in the recent era, and neither is stable across it.

**Opening-auction penalty (PROXY, extra one-way bps charged to the open arm only):**

| extra bps | 10-month gap (*t*) | 20-week gap (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 (headline) | +37.0 (+1.53) | −26.1 (−0.80) |
| +1 | +35.1 (+1.46) | −31.5 (−0.97) |
| +2 | +33.2 (+1.38) | −36.8 (−1.13) |
| +5 | +27.5 (+1.15) | −52.9 (−1.62) |

Both rules drift toward the close as the assumed opening spread widens — as they must, since
the opening auction is the wider of the two.

**Cash-split PROXY (SPY, 10-month):** gap = −4.87 / −4.84 / −4.85 / −4.89 bps/yr at overnight
shares 0.00 / 0.50 / 0.73 / 1.00 (*t* = −0.157 throughout). The assumption is inert, as a ~1
bp/day accrual must be.

## Mechanism — why the sliver averages out

Mean **intraday (price-only)** return on trade days, 10-month rule:

| Tape | entry days | exit days | all days | entry − exit (Welch *t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | +31.9 bps (n=16) | +39.8 bps (n=15) | +1.91 bps | −7.9 (−0.22) |
| IWM | +0.9 bps (n=19) | −50.4 bps (n=18) | +0.05 bps | +51.2 (+1.06) |
| EEM | +48.0 bps (n=19) | −17.1 bps (n=18) | +1.33 bps | +65.1 (**+2.51**) |
| EFA | +25.2 bps (n=17) | −13.5 bps (n=16) | +3.23 bps | +38.7 (+1.68) |

Entries and exits alternate, so a *constant* intraday drift would cancel exactly over a full
cycle; a venue edge needs the two conditional means to differ. On the 20-week rule — the same
tapes, three times the trades — every one of the four spreads flips **negative** (−15.4, −6.4,
−9.9, −9.4 bps, all |*t*| < 0.9). The monthly spread is a small-sample artefact, not a
mechanism.

## Dispersion — what the coin flip actually costs you

Across the 8 rule × tape cells the realised gap has **mean +5.4 bps/yr, sd 39.5 bps/yr, range
[−35.8, +66.6]**, and clears |*t*| = 2 in **1 of 8** cells (about what eight independent draws
produce by chance). So the venue choice buys **no** expected return but adds roughly **±0.4
pp/yr of track-record noise** — a free coin flip that can decorate or ruin a back-test.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

The generator splits a *fixed* close-to-close path into overnight and intraday legs, so the
close-executed arm is bit-identical across the knob and only the open arm can move.

| World | Gap (mean of 8 seeds) | HAC *t* (mean) | fires |*t*| ≥ 2 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Planted intraday continuation | **+134.6 bps/yr** (sd 28.2) | **+3.84** | **8/8** |
| Null (split randomised) | +13.8 bps/yr (sd 38.4) | +0.55 | 1/8 |

The detector recovers a planted venue edge on every seed and stays at the nominal false-positive
rate on the null — so the real-tape zero is a fact about the tape, not a dead harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** The venue gap is noise. Pooled over all **538 fills** (on 361 distinct
  dates) the open-versus-close slippage is **+1.39 bps per trade**, *t* = +0.33 naive and
  **+0.23 clustered on the trade date**, and the open fill wins **49.6%** of the time —
  95% Wilson [45.4%, 53.8%], cluster-bootstrap **[44.1%, 55.1%]**. The two rules print
  **opposite signs** (+37.0 bps/yr monthly,
  *t* = +1.53; −26.1 bps/yr weekly, *t* = −0.80) on the same tapes over the same window, both
  bootstrap CIs straddle zero, and the era cut disagrees with itself. The single |*t*| ≥ 2 cell
  (EEM monthly, +66.6 bps/yr, 37 trades) is one significant result out of eight draws, and the
  mechanism behind it — a positive entry-minus-exit intraday spread — reverses sign on the
  higher-powered weekly rule. *Survivorship: none — four continuously listed index ETFs, no
  cross-section, no membership screen; the price-only/total-return split is labelled per leg.*
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is nothing to bank. The gap has no reliable sign, so no
  venue rule can be written down in advance; the +0.031 monthly Sharpe advantage of the open
  fill is mirrored by a −0.021 weekly disadvantage. What *is* robust is the dispersion: the
  choice adds ~±0.4 pp/yr of pure track-record luck. And once the opening auction is charged
  its real (wider) spread, both rules move toward the **close** — so the honest operating
  advice is a cost argument, not an alpha one: fill in the closing auction because it is
  cheaper and deeper, and expect exactly zero return for it.
